strengths: The core idea (have the LLM generate a random string as an internal entropy source, then deterministically map it to a sample) is simple, elegant, and broadly applicable, requiring no model access or architectural changes.

Extensive and well-designed experiments: five frontier LLMs, five PIF settings, strong baselines (temperature, few-shot, prompt ensemble, sequential sampling with history, external randomized seed ablation), and a PRNG reference point; SSoT approaches PRNG-level fidelity, which is a convincing result.

The theoretical analysis is a genuine added value: Theorem 4.1 (via Leftover Hash Lemma over delta-SV sources) and Theorem 4.2 (Fourier/Plancherel analysis of the sum-mod strategy) give meaningful insight into why lengthening the string improves distributional fidelity even under autoregressive correlations.

The mechanism analysis is particularly interesting: showing that LLMs autonomously converge on sum-mod vs. rolling-hash strategies depending on whether the target is uniform or biased, and that PIF quality scales with CoT length (Fig. 7), provides a mechanistic explanation beyond black-box gains.

Practical demonstrations (adversarial RPS against pattern-exploiting bots, NoveltyBench diversity without utility loss) show real-world relevance, including for reasoning models where temperature cannot be tuned.
High reproducibility: full prompts, bot lists, evaluation details, and extended results (KL/TV) are in the appendix; the method itself requires only a prompt addition.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially a prompt-engineering trick; the key insight (LLMs are bad at sampling but decent at deterministic string manipulation) is plausible and the contribution, while well executed, is incremental.

Practical significance is debatable: whenever an external PRNG or tool call is available, it trivially dominates SSoT at zero inference cost; SSoT's advantage is confined to contexts where no external randomness is accessible, and it incurs substantial extra CoT tokens.

Theory-practice gap: the delta-SV source assumption and the independence assumption in the sum-mod theorem are not verified against actual LLM-generated strings, and the paper does not measure how far real strings deviate from these assumptions; the bounds may be loose or vacuous in practice.

Effectiveness is strongly tied to long-CoT reasoning models; gains on weaker/non-reasoning models (deepseek-v3, gpt-4o in some settings) are modest, limiting generality, and the added token cost of the method is not analyzed or reported.

DAG evaluation is comparatively thin: only one model (deepseek-r1), one benchmark (NoveltyBench), and diversity measured via Distinct; no human or stronger quality evaluation, and the claim that quality is preserved rests on Utility scores alone.
K=100 samples per empirical distribution is small for distributional fidelity claims, particularly for the biased 9-choice setting; statistical significance of the differences is not tested.
CoT strategy classification relies on an LLM judge (gemini-2.5-flash) without human validation of the taxonomy, adding an unquantified source of noise to the mechanism analysis.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the proposed SSoT prompting technique is simple, general, and easy to apply to any LLM without additional tooling or fine-tuning.

The empirical evaluation of PIF is fairly broad: five frontier LLMs, multiple target distributions, JS/KL/TV metrics with repeated trials, and sensible baselines including temperature scaling, few-shot examples, prompt ensembles, sequential sampling, and an external-seed ablation.

The theoretical analysis (leftover hash lemma over delta-SV sources, plus a Fourier-analytic bound for the sum-mod strategy) is a nice touch and provides a plausible explanation for why long random strings help, and the CoT-length scaling analysis (Figure 7) connects the theory to observed behavior.
The adversarial Rock-Paper-Scissors experiment against pattern-exploiting bots is a fun and relevant demonstration of a practical use case for mixed-strategy play.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core observation that LLMs are biased when sampling from distributions, and the idea of extracting randomness from a self-generated seed, builds directly on a large body of prior work the authors themselves cite (Hopkins et al., 2023; Meister et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; van Koevering & Kleinberg, 2024). The contribution amounts to a one-line system-prompt trick plus standard tools (leftover hash lemma, Weissman et al. bound, Plancherel); the theory confirms intuition rather than yielding new insight.

The key theoretical assumptions are unverified in practice. The delta-SV source condition (conditional probabilities bounded away from degeneracy) on autoregressively LLM-generated characters is assumed, not shown; no empirical measurement of delta or the min-entropy of generated strings is provided. The theory also assumes independence across the K sampled strings, but parallel SSoT calls at temperature 0.6 could share systematic mode collapse, and this is never tested.

The diversity-aware generation evaluation is thin: only one model (deepseek-r1), one benchmark family (NoveltyBench), and 'Distinct' measured over just 8 samples per prompt. Whether SSoT preserves or improves quality (Utility) is unclear — Utility is parenthesized but never analyzed, and 'Utility' on NoveltyBench is an LLM-judged metric subject to bias, potentially confounded by SSoT's longer, more structured outputs.

The method's effectiveness appears to hinge on long CoT reasoning traces (best results on deepseek-r1/QwQ-32B with long reasoning), so the method is expensive at inference time, yet token/compute cost and latency overhead of SSoT versus temperature or prompt ensembling are never reported. For non-reasoning models the reported gains are far smaller (e.g., o4-mini-high in Table 1).

The RPS experiment uses only 10 bots with a single 100-game match each (no repetition or significance testing), and the box plot in Figure 4 shows substantial overlap between SSoT and Baseline; the claim that SSoT enables mixed-strategy play is weakly supported by this design.

Prompt design confounds: the SSoT system prompts embed extra instructions beyond the random-string trick (e.g., 'select ONE move using Nash equilibrium strategies'), so it is unclear how much of the RPS gain comes from the seed versus the added strategy guidance. The ablation in 5.1.2 partially addresses this for PIF but not for RPS or DAG.

Significance is narrow: the PIF task is an interesting diagnostic but of limited practical impact, and for DAG the same effect could plausibly be achieved by simply asking the model to vary its answer or by standard sampling; no comparison against simpler diversity heuristics (e.g., 'vary your response', constraint-based diversity methods from the related work) is provided.

The CoT strategy analysis (Section 5.3) relies on an LLM classifier (gemini-2.5-flash) whose accuracy is never validated against human labels, so all mechanistic claims about Sum-Mod vs. Rolling Hash strategies rest on an unverified automated annotation.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated method (SSoT) addressing a clearly identified and practically important problem: LLMs fail to sample from explicit target distributions and produce collapsed outputs, which matters for behavioral simulation, mixed-strategy play, and test-time scaling diversity.

Extensive and convincing PIF evaluation: five frontier models (including reasoning models with inaccessible temperature), multiple task configurations, three divergence metrics (JS in main text, KL and TV in appendix), and a PRNG reference that makes 'approaching ideal' claims concrete and verifiable.

Strong baseline coverage: temperature sweeps, few-shot with fixed/random examples, prompt ensembling with randomized action orders, sequential sampling with history, and an external-seed ablation that cleanly isolates where the gains come from (the model's own string manipulation vs. mere randomness supply).
Well-designed adversarial RPS experiment against pattern-exploiting bots that demonstrates practical utility of faithful sampling, not just distributional metrics.

Genuine mechanistic insight: the CoT analysis reveals emergent extraction strategies (sum-mod vs. rolling hash) that qualitatively differ between unbiased and biased settings, and the CoT-scaling analysis links string entropy to reasoning length, connecting the empirical gains to model behavior.

Theory is relevant rather than decorative: bounds via the Leftover Hash Lemma over δ-SV sources (allowing autoregressive correlations) and a Fourier-analytic bound for the exact sum-mod strategy observed in the CoT analysis; the appendix proofs appear careful and the extension to biased targets is handled.
Transparent disclosure of LLM usage and clear writing overall.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty of the core technique: 'generate a random string and use it' is an intuitive fix, and the surrounding phenomenon (LLMs fail at random selection, positional biases, RPS gaps) is already documented in Meister et al. (2025), Gu et al. (2025), Hopkins et al. (2023), Van Koevering & Kleinberg (2024), and the Anonymous (2025) RPS work cited by the authors themselves. The contribution is an effective engineering remedy plus analysis rather than a new scientific insight.

The theory largely re-derives known results (LHL + Weissman et al. empirical bounds; Plancherel-based random-walk analysis following Diaconis & Shahshahani) under assumptions that may not hold for actual LLM strings: Theorem 4.1 requires the hash function to be sampled uniformly at random from a 2-universal family, whereas LLMs choose a deterministic strategy; Theorem 4.2 assumes independent characters and prime M. The paper does not empirically validate how close real LLM-generated strings are to the δ-SV or independence assumptions.

Robustness concerns remain: QwQ-32B regresses on the 2-choice task (JS up 40%), showing the method is not uniformly reliable, and the paper does not characterize when or why SSoT fails. Performance for non-reasoning models, while improved, still lags far behind PRNG.

Evaluation scale and cost are under-reported: K=100 trials with 10 repetitions on a small set of task types; no significance testing beyond means and standard deviations; no accounting of the token/compute overhead of the inflated SSoT CoT, which is a practical concern since the method relies on long reasoning traces.

DAG evaluation is comparatively thin: a single model (deepseek-r1), one benchmark (NoveltyBench), eight generations per prompt, and no human or additional-judge validation of quality beyond the benchmark's own utility metric; some categories show utility drops relative to baselines.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the prompt-engineering results and the CoT classification pipeline (itself LLM-based and unvalidated against human labels beyond manual prompt construction).

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'approaching the ideal performance of a PRNG' holds only for the two long-CoT models, and the diversity benefit on WildChat lacks the ablation/baseline breadth of the curated-dataset experiments.

strengths: The proposed SSoT method is extremely simple, requires no training or tuning, and is applicable via a single system-prompt modification, making it immediately practical for APIs where temperature/seed control is unavailable (e.g., o4-mini).

Very comprehensive empirical evaluation: five frontier LLMs across five PIF settings, a wide action-space sweep (2 to 64 choices), and strong baselines including temperature scaling, few-shot exemplars, 50-prompt ensembling with randomized action order, sequential sampling with history, and external (injected) seeds. SSoT consistently achieves near-PRNG JS divergence, which is a compelling result.

The theoretical analysis is well-motivated and connected to practice: the TV-distance bound for δ-Santha-Vazirani sources via the Leftover Hash Lemma and the spectral/random-walk analysis of the sum-mod strategy (which LLMs actually adopt, per the CoT analysis) nicely bridge theory and observed LLM behavior, and the n-dependence is empirically validated (Table 7, Figure 3).

The analysis sections are a genuine contribution: CoT strategy classification (sum-mod vs. rolling hash adapting to biased/unbiased targets), CoT-length scaling of randomness quality (budget-forcing experiments at T=0 with LZ complexity), failure-case analysis of QwQ-32B (positional bias in generated strings), and the demonstration that LLMs can produce high-entropy strings through internal reasoning alone at T=0 are insightful.

Beyond closed-set PIF, the paper demonstrates value on open-ended diversity (NoveltyBench, both curated and WildChat) and an adversarial RPS setting against pattern-exploiting bots, supporting the breadth of the claims.

Reproducibility is strong: all prompts are provided, experimental settings (temperatures, K, repetitions) are specified, and limitations (small-model failures, bias propagation, single-answer tasks) are candidly discussed.
weaknesses: The core mechanism's novelty is limited: 'ask the model to generate a random string and reason over it' is a straightforward prompting idea. The main intellectual content is in the analysis rather than the method itself, and the theorems are largely careful compositions of known results (Leftover Hash Lemma, Weissman et al., Diaconis-Shahshahani) rather than new techniques.

The entropy source is not fully characterized. If the string is sampled at temperature T>0, the 'new' randomness largely comes from the same decoding stochasticity the baseline has; the paper does not rigorously compare against the natural baseline of directly sampling the answer token from the model's distribution with adjusted logits, nor explain precisely why long strings improve uniformity beyond what token sampling provides. The T=0 experiments partially address this, but the mechanism remains only partially explained.

Statistical granularity is thin: all headline results use K=100 samples repeated 10 times. At this scale the finite-sample floor is large, and several comparisons (e.g., QwQ-32B 2-choice where SSoT is worse, parity with PRNG claims) would benefit from significance testing and larger K. 'Approaching PRNG' claims should be qualified accordingly.

Cost/latency of the method is not quantified in the main text. SSoT induces long CoTs (often thousands of thinking tokens plus a random string) per query; a tokens-per-query or cost-accuracy trade-off analysis against baselines like prompt ensembling or external seed injection is missing and is essential for judging practical significance.

Robustness of the internal randomness is a known weakness acknowledged only partially: the QwQ failure case (947/1000 strings starting with '7') shows the generated 'seed' can be highly biased, and the method depends on the model choosing a sound extraction strategy. The paper offers mitigation via prompt steering but no systematic solution.

The DAG gains, while consistent, are moderate (Distinct 4.70→6.19 overall) and measured with a classifier-based equivalence metric whose sensitivity to the SSoT-induced stylistic template usage is not analyzed; Utility changes are mixed across categories, so 'diversity without quality loss' could be stated more cautiously.

The theory assumes uniform targets with biased targets handled only via a rounding/quantization argument (Appendix G.6), and Theorem 4.2 assumes independent characters, with dependent cases deferred to 'standard mixing assumptions' that are not worked out, leaving a gap between the theorems and the actual autoregressive setting for the sum-mod strategy.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem: LLMs exhibit systematic biases when asked to sample from target distributions (PIF) or to produce diverse open-ended responses (DAG), with clear downstream applications (human simulation, game play, test-time scaling).

The empirical evaluation is extensive: five frontier LLMs, five PIF settings, comparisons against strong baselines (high temperature, few-shot, prompt ensembling, sequential sampling, external seed injection, tool calls), an adversarial Rock-Paper-Scissors application, and NoveltyBench diversity experiments.

The theoretical analysis (generalizing Santha-Vazirani sources to non-binary alphabets, Leftover Hash Lemma application, and a Fourier/random-walk bound for the sum-mod strategy) connects the observed LLM strategies (sum-mod, rolling hash) to formal guarantees, and the theory is validated empirically via string-length ablations and CoT-length scaling analysis.
The paper includes valuable diagnostic analyses: LLM-as-classifier strategy breakdowns, string complexity measurements at T=0, failure analysis of QwQ-32B, and a candid limitations section.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core contribution: the method is a simple prompt addition ('generate a random string and manipulate it'). Prior work on LLM randomness biases (Hopkins et al., 2023; Van Koevering & Kleinberg, 2024; Meister et al., 2025) and on diversity enhancement is substantial, and the delta over injecting an external PRNG seed appears small (e.g., Seed Injection 6.00 vs. SSoT 6.19 Overall Distinct on NoveltyBench; the external randomized seed baseline performs comparably in unbiased PIF).

A fundamental confound is not fully resolved: at nonzero temperature the decoding process already supplies entropy, so it is unclear how much of the improvement comes from the internally 'reasoned' random string versus the stochastic sampling that would occur anyway. The T=0 experiment (Fig. 7c) partially addresses this but is not integrated into the main PIF/DAG results, where temperature was not controlled to 0.

The theoretical results are largely applications of well-known tools (Leftover Hash Lemma, Weissman et al. inequality, Diaconis & Shahshahani spectral analysis); the assumptions (δ-SV condition) are only approximately verified in practice, and the sum-mod analysis requires independence assumptions that LLM-generated strings evidently violate.

Practical significance and cost are not analyzed: SSoT substantially increases output length (long random strings plus CoT), yet no token-cost/latency comparison against the cheaper external-seed baseline is reported; the paper also shows the method fails on small models and can even hurt performance in some settings (QwQ-32B 2-choice; Qwen3-4B/1.7B).

Some claims overstate the evidence: 'approaching the ideal performance of a pseudo-random number generator' holds only for the strongest reasoning models on selected tasks; DAG improvements rest on a single model (deepseek-r1) and a benchmark with LLM-based utility judgments, raising generalizability and reproducibility concerns.

The CoT strategy analysis relies on LLM classifiers (gemini-2.5-flash) without validation of classification accuracy against human labels, so the strategy percentages (Figures 5, 6, 13, 14) carry unquantified uncertainty.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly defined problem (Probabilistic Instruction Following and Diversity-Aware Generation) with concrete applications in simulation, gaming, and test-time scaling

Very extensive empirical evaluation: five frontier LLMs, multiple baselines (temperature, few-shot, prompt ensembling, sequential sampling, external seed injection, tool calls), ablations, an adversarial RPS game demonstration, and NoveltyBench for open-ended diversity
Simple, practical method requiring only a prompt change, with a demonstrated simplified-prompt variant and support for models where temperature is not adjustable

Genuine theoretical contribution: extension of the Leftover Hash Lemma framework to non-binary Santha-Vazirani sources with autoregressive correlation, plus a spectral bound for the sum-mod strategy that LLMs actually employ, validated empirically in the CoT analysis (Appendix E)

Insightful mechanistic analyses: LLMs autonomously adopt sum-mod vs. rolling-hash strategies depending on task complexity, and PIF performance scales with reasoning (CoT) length, supported by careful budget-forcing and string-complexity experiments
Honest limitations section and failure analysis (e.g., QwQ-32B bias propagation case), and comprehensive appendices with full prompts enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: The core method is a fairly simple prompting trick; the headline results, while strong, may be seen as incremental over the known observation that LLMs fail distributional sampling (Meister et al. 2025; Gu et al. 2025; the cited anonymous RPS work), and the theoretical results largely assemble known tools (Leftover Hash Lemma, Weissman et al., Diaconis-Shahshahani)

The 'randomness' is ultimately inherited from decoding stochasticity; the framing of 'approaching PRNG' could invite scrutiny since SSoT does not create new entropy, only debiases the mapping from sampled outputs, and the paper could discuss this more explicitly

Evaluation is based on only 10 repetitions of K=100 samples per configuration; some reported differences (e.g., PRNG row comparisons) have overlapping error bars, and statistical significance is not reported
CoT strategy classification relies on gemini-2.5-flash as an LLM judge without human validation of classification accuracy, which weakens the strategy-analysis claims

Dependence on strong reasoning capability limits generality: the method fails or even degrades performance on small models (Qwen3-4B/1.7B show large regressions on some tasks) and in specific failure modes, as the authors themselves acknowledge
The performance peak at n=24 and degradation for longer strings (Table 7) somewhat contradicts the clean theoretical monotonicity story, and the explanation (arithmetic errors) is post-hoc
